author: baparker
title: Floyd County considering incentive pay for CDL holders, certified employees - NewsBreak
text:
By baparker ,
8 hours ago Jamie McCord Floyd County officials are considering a new incentive pay system that would provide additional compensation to employees who hold commercial driver’s licenses and other professional certifications, even when those credentials are not required for their positions.
County Manager Jamie McCord said the idea is part of a broader effort to address pay equity and better utilize employee skills across departments.
McCord said the county’s current pay structure is based strictly on job classifications and pay grades, with no added compensation for employees who bring extra certifications to their roles.
“At this point, we don’t have an incentive pay,” McCord said. “You’re hired in the job category that you’re in, and then the job description dictates what you have.”
Under the proposed change, employees whose jobs require certifications such as a CDL would not receive additional pay for those credentials. However, workers who obtain certifications that are not required for their positions — but are still used by the county — could receive extra compensation.
“If it’s required, you don’t get the additional pay,” McCord said. “But if it’s not required and you have it and we’re utilizing it, they deserve some form of compensation.”
The idea extends beyond commercial driver’s licenses. County officials are also looking at other certifications and licenses held by employees, including pesticide applicator licenses, pool operator certifications and arborist credentials.
McCord said the effort is intended to simplify what has become a wide range of job requirements and certifications across departments.
“We have other licensing and other certifications that are required throughout the county and some that people have that are not required,” he said.
He pointed to equipment operator positions as an example, noting that some employees classified as EO-1s are not required to hold a CDL but still possess one and use it in their work.
“That’s where it needs to be,” McCord said. “We can utilize that license, and we need to compensate people that are not required to have it.”
County officials have also invested in expanding the number of certified drivers through internal training programs, including CDL certification efforts led within the Public Works Department. McCord said the county has spent about $20,000 during the past two years on training and has seen strong retention among employees who completed the program.
“You want to get a return on your investment,” he said. “You hope they stay with you for a period of time at least.”
While retention has improved, McCord said the incentive pay proposal is meant to ensure employees are recognized for additional skills that benefit county operations.
The plan would likely apply countywide if adopted, potentially affecting multiple departments beyond Public Works and water services, including public safety and administrative offices.
“There may be other skill sets that (the police department) has and or clerk’s office certifications,” McCord said.
Officials said the proposal is still in development, with details such as pay amounts yet to be determined. If approved, it would most likely be considered during the next budget cycle, with implementation targeted for 2027.
McCord said the goal is to create a more consistent and fair system that compensates employees for skills the county actively uses.
“That’s what we’re trying to do,” he said. “Just making sure people are getting compensated for the work they’re actually doing.”

He pointed to equipment operator positions as an example, noting that some employees classified as EO-1s are not required to hold a CDL but still possess one and use it in their work.
